title: How Big Tech is likely to respond
full_text:
Critics warn the “opt-in” model for algorithms on social media that Labor is weighing up could trigger a chaotic transition toward paid subscriptions or degraded content feeds rather than a safer internet.
The government is considering releasing a draft on its proposed digital duty-of-care bill, attempting to pass laws that will increase fines on social media giants for flouting the ban on child users. It is also meeting with executives at artificial intelligence companies to consult on its proposed legal framework for regulating the technology.
The Australian understands the digital duty-of-care draft, expected to be released on Tuesday, does not include a proposed model to regulate algorithms, which curate users’ content by tracking their online behaviour. But it is expected to refer to a new government role in providing users choice over algorithms.
Australian Computer Society professional ethics committee vice-chair Emilia Bellucci says advertising has become a multi-billion dollar industry for social media companies and they are unlikely to give that up.
This means Australians are likely to face three options if they opt out of algorithms. The first – and most unlikely – is going back to seeing only what their friends and connections post. This is what Facebook, Instagram and other platforms offered originally.
The second is social media companies stuffing feeds with lower quality, sponsored and untargeted content to make up for advertising losses. Lastly, social media giants could consider introducing paid subscriptions.
“When it comes to revenue, it’s all about the ads and it’s about how targeted the ads are,” said Dr Bellucci, who is also a senior lecturer at Deakin Business School.
‘So, the more that we spend time on the platforms, the better the ads will be, and hence the advertisers will be happy. So, if they’re removing that, they’re going to need to make the money elsewhere, and it could be where we are given worse content.
“(Opting out) could mean you see maybe just friends are posting, but nothing more than that. And I don’t know if that’s a good or bad thing. They could (also) turn more to subscription based. They already had those sort of models ... YouTube Premium, that kind of thing.” But Dr Bellucci, while welcoming the government’s efforts to make the internet safer, questioned how effective the proposed opt-out measure would be in curbing harms. She said opting in might be a better option.
“The more vulnerable (people) in our populations, the young adults even, don’t have the capacity to understand that this (algorithm) is actually not them.
“They’re just going down that rabbit hole because it makes them feel good because they’re in that state, and they’re the ones that are less likely to opt out.” Sarah Wynn-Williams – a former director of global public policy at Facebook turned whistleblower – told a US Senate inquiry last year the tech titan could identify when a child was “feeling worthless”.
“They will take that information and share it with advertisers. One of the things about advertising is advertisers understand that when people don’t feel good about themselves, it’s often a good time to pitch a product – you know, people are more likely to buy something,” Ms Wynne-Williams said.
Swinburne media expert Belinda Barnet said: “Children aged under 16 should not be exposed to these products at all, but over 16s should be able to choose if they’d like the content displayed in this way” and agreed opting in instead of opting out might be a better approach. If the system is opt-in then people are required to at least think about it,” he said.
Monash University’s Rashina Hoda said an opt-out option may “not always be accessible or implementable”.
“For example, users may not even know they are in an echo chamber and therefore may not be able to help themselves,” Professor Hoda said.
“This could be even more challenging for vulnerable groups, including young people, the elderly and users with mental health conditions. “Although it comes with its own challenges, such as the loss of personalised content, an opt-in option would provide a stronger control setting for users.”
